BEDSIDE TESTS__Vital Signs & Observation:
Basic observations ("obs") are the routine bedside vital signs recorded on every acute inpatient. In UK practice they are aggregated into the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2), a validated track-and-trigger tool that converts six physiological parameters into a single number to flag clinical deterioration early and standardise the escalation response.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why we score obs

Deterioration in acutely unwell patients is usually preceded by measurable derangement of vital signs hours before an arrest or ICU admission. Aggregating them removes reliance on any single reassuring value and catches the compensating patient whose parameters are each "borderline" but collectively worrying. NEWS2 (RCP, 2017) is mandated across NHS acute trusts to give one common language for illness severity and escalation.

🫁Respiratory rate
Earliest and most sensitive marker of deterioration
🩸SpO₂
Peripheral oxygen saturation (Scale 1 or 2)
💨Air vs O₂
Supplemental oxygen scores 2 points
🩺Systolic BP
Systolic pressure only (not diastolic/MAP)
❤️Pulse
Heart rate — both brady- and tachycardia score
🧠Consciousness
ACVPU — new confusion counts as abnormal
🌡️Temperature
Both hypo- and hyperthermia score
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — measuring & scoring

Each of the six parameters is assigned 0, 1, 2 or 3 points based on how far it deviates from normal; supplemental oxygen adds a further 2 points, and the individual scores are summed to give the aggregate NEWS2. Crucially, respiratory rate must be counted over a full 60 seconds (not estimated), and SpO₂ is read on the correct scale for the patient.

Respiratory rate: ≤8 or ≥25 scores 3; 21–24 scores 2; 9–11 scores 1; 12–20 is normal (0).
SpO₂ (Scale 1): ≤91% scores 3; 92–93% scores 2; 94–95% scores 1; ≥96% is normal (0).
Oxygen: any supplemental O₂ = 2; breathing air = 0.
Systolic BP: ≤90 or ≥220 scores 3; 91–100 scores 2; 101–110 scores 1; 111–219 is normal (0).
Pulse: ≤40 or ≥131 scores 3; 111–130 scores 2; 41–50 or 91–110 scores 1; 51–90 is normal (0).
Consciousness (ACVPU): Alert = 0; new Confusion, Voice, Pain or Unresponsive = 3.
Temperature: ≤35.0°C scores 3; ≥39.1°C scores 2; 35.1–36.0 or 38.1–39.0 scores 1; 36.1–38.0°C is normal (0).
3INTERPRETATION — thresholds & escalation

The aggregate score maps to a defined monitoring frequency and clinical response. Any single parameter scoring 3 (a "red score") is significant even if the total is low.

Total 0→Routine monitoring, minimum 12-hourly
Total 1–4 (low)→Assess by registered nurse, 4–6-hourly obs
Any single parameter = 3 (low-medium)→Urgent review by ward doctor, min 1-hourly obs
Total 5–6 (medium)→Urgent review, consider sepsis screen, min 1-hourly obs
Total ≥7 (high)→Emergency assessment by critical-care team, continuous monitoring
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SpO₂ SCALE 2

NEWS2 introduced SpO₂ Scale 2 for patients with hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure who have an agreed target saturation of 88–92% (typically COPD). On Scale 2, a saturation of 88–92% on air scores 0, and — counter-intuitively — high saturations on oxygen score points, because over-oxygenation is dangerous in these patients. Scale 2 must only be applied when specified by a competent clinician and clearly documented.

NEWS2 is not validated in pregnancy (use a modified obstetric score, e.g. MEOWS) or in children (use PEWS).
It is a trigger to think, not a diagnosis — clinical judgement can escalate care regardless of the number.
A patient can be seriously ill with a low score (e.g. isolated severe hyponatraemia or ischaemia), so never let a normal NEWS override concern.
🚩 A single parameter scoring 3 (e.g. RR ≥25, SpO₂ ≤91%, or new confusion) mandates urgent clinical review even when the aggregate score is otherwise low — an isolated red score is an independent trigger and must never be "averaged away" by reassuring vitals.
🎓 A NEWS2 of ≥5 is the recognised threshold that should prompt a sepsis screen and urgent senior review — remember "5 = think sepsis". In hypercapnic patients, always confirm whether Scale 1 or Scale 2 is in use before interpreting the SpO₂ score.

Pulse assessment is a foundational bedside examination: by palpating a peripheral artery (usually the radial) you read off the heart's rate, rhythm, volume and character, plus comparisons between sites. A skilled hand can flag atrial fibrillation, aortic valve disease, cardiac tamponade and aortic coarctation before a single investigation is ordered.

1Indication & principle

Every cardiovascular examination begins with the pulse because the arterial waveform is a direct transmission of left-ventricular ejection into the aorta. The rate reflects sinoatrial/conduction activity, the rhythm reflects electrical regularity, and the volume and character reflect stroke volume and the state of the aortic valve and vessels. Because the pulse encodes both electrical and mechanical information at once, it is the quickest screen for arrhythmia, valvular disease and haemodynamic compromise.

Rate = how fast (beats per minute)
Rhythm = regular vs irregular
Volume/character = the shape and force of the upstroke
2How it is performed

Use the pulps of two or three fingers (never the thumb, which has its own pulse) over the radial artery at the lateral volar wrist. Count for a full 30 seconds and double (or 60 seconds if irregular). Assess:

Rate — count beats over time
Rhythm — regular, regularly irregular, or irregularly irregular
Volume & character — best felt at the larger brachial or carotid arteries

Then perform site comparisons: palpate both radials simultaneously (radio-radial delay) and a radial with a femoral pulse (radio-femoral delay). The carotid is the site of choice for judging character because it is central and large.

3Interpretation — rate, rhythm, character

The normal adult resting rate is 60–100 bpm. Rhythm and character then localise pathology:

Rate < 60 bpm→Bradycardia (fitness, drugs, heart block, hypothyroidism)
Rate > 100 bpm→Tachycardia (sepsis, pain, hypovolaemia, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis)
Irregularly irregular→Atrial fibrillation (until proven otherwise)
Slow-rising, low-volume→Aortic stenosis
Collapsing / water-hammer→Aortic regurgitation
Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall on inspiration)→Cardiac tamponade or severe acute asthma
Pulsus alternans (alternating strong/weak beats)→Severe LV systolic failure
Radio-femoral delay→Coarctation of the aorta
Radio-radial delay / asymmetry→Aortic dissection or subclavian stenosis
🫀Slow-rising
Aortic stenosis — delayed, sustained upstroke
💧Collapsing
Aortic regurgitation — brisk rise, rapid fall
🌬️Paradoxus
Tamponade / severe asthma
🔁Alternans
Severe LV failure
4Pitfalls, limitations & the apex-radial deficit

The radial pulse can underestimate the true heart rate. In atrial fibrillation, weak beats generated by inadequate ventricular filling fail to open the aortic valve enough to transmit a palpable radial pulse — producing an apex-radial (pulse) deficit, where the rate auscultated at the apex exceeds the rate palpated at the wrist.

Apex rate > radial rate→Pulse deficit — classic of AF; always count the apex, not the wrist, for true rate
A regular pulse does not exclude ectopics — confirm with an ECG
Peripheral vasoconstriction (shock, cold) makes distal pulses feel weak and slow-rising falsely
Character is unreliable at the radial — assess it centrally at the carotid
🚩 An irregularly irregular pulse is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise. AF confers a major thromboembolic stroke risk — do not dismiss it. Confirm with a 12-lead ECG and assess stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) for anticoagulation.
🎓 To distinguish AF from multiple ectopics at the bedside: ectopic beats disappear on exercise (the sinus rate overtakes them and the pulse becomes regular), whereas AF stays irregularly irregular. A true collapsing pulse is confirmed by raising the patient's arm above the head while palpating the radial with your palm.

Blood pressure (BP) measurement is a core bedside skill that quantifies arterial pressure to screen for and diagnose hypertension, guide fluid and haemodynamic management, and detect hypotension. It is performed either by manual auscultation with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope, or by an automated oscillometric device. Correct technique is essential: small errors in cuff size, arm position or method translate directly into misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment.

1Indication & principle

BP is measured to screen for and stage hypertension, monitor treatment, assess acutely unwell or shocked patients, and detect postural hypotension. The cuff occludes the brachial artery; as pressure is released, blood flow resumes turbulently, generating audible Korotkoff sounds (auscultatory method) or oscillations in cuff pressure (oscillometric method).

Systolic pressure = pressure at which pulsatile flow first returns.
Diastolic pressure = pressure at which flow becomes fully laminar (silent).
2How it is performed

The patient should be seated and relaxed for several minutes, with the arm supported at heart level and the bladder of the cuff encircling ~80% of the arm circumference. First estimate systolic pressure by palpation (inflate until the radial pulse disappears) to avoid missing an auscultatory gap, then inflate 20–30 mmHg above this. Deflate slowly (2–3 mmHg/second) while auscultating over the brachial artery.

🔊Korotkoff I
First tapping sound = systolic BP
🔉Korotkoff V
Disappearance of sound = diastolic BP
🤖Oscillometric
Automated device detects arterial oscillations
✋Palpatory
Estimates systolic only; avoids auscultatory gap

Automated oscillometric devices measure the mean arterial pressure directly and compute systolic/diastolic values algorithmically; they are unreliable in atrial fibrillation, where manual auscultation is preferred.

3Interpretation & NICE thresholds

A raised clinic reading should be confirmed with ambulatory (ABPM) or home (HBPM) monitoring, which use lower thresholds because they exclude the white-coat effect (BP elevated by the clinical setting).

Clinic BP ≥140/90 mmHg→Suspected hypertension — offer ABPM/HBPM to confirm
ABPM/HBPM average ≥135/85 mmHg→Stage 1 hypertension confirmed
Clinic ≥160/100 & ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95 mmHg→Stage 2 hypertension — offer drug treatment at any age
Clinic BP ≥180/120 mmHg→Severe hypertension — assess for end-organ damage
Large white-coat effect→Clinic > out-of-clinic BP; use ABPM/HBPM to guide decisions
4Pitfalls & limitations
A cuff that is too small for the arm overestimates BP; a cuff too large underestimates it.
An unsupported arm or arm below heart level falsely raises the reading (~1–2 mmHg per cm below the heart).
Deflating too quickly underestimates systolic and overestimates diastolic pressure.
An auscultatory gap (temporary disappearance of sounds) can cause underestimation of systolic BP if palpation is skipped.
Measure in both arms on first assessment; a sustained difference >15 mmHg warrants investigation.
🚩 Using the wrong cuff size (too small) can spuriously label a normotensive patient as hypertensive. More urgently, a clinic BP ≥180/120 mmHg with signs of retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema (accelerated/malignant hypertension) or new confusion, chest pain or acute kidney injury requires same-day specialist assessment, not routine ABPM.
🎓 Korotkoff I = systolic, Korotkoff V (disappearance) = diastolic. Always palpate the systolic first to avoid the auscultatory gap, and remember NICE confirms hypertension with ABPM/HBPM at the lower ≥135/85 threshold, not the clinic ≥140/90 figure.

Respiratory rate (RR) is the number of breaths taken in one full minute and, together with the visible work of breathing, is the most sensitive bedside marker of how hard a patient is fighting to oxygenate and clear CO₂. It is the first vital sign to drift when a patient deteriorates from sepsis, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, PE, metabolic acidosis or opioid toxicity — yet it is the most frequently mis-counted or fabricated observation on the ward.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why RR is the sentinel sign

Ventilation is tightly controlled by central and peripheral chemoreceptors responding to CO₂, H⁺ and O₂. When gas exchange fails or a metabolic acid load accumulates, the medulla drives ventilation up before heart rate, blood pressure or conscious level change — because these are defended by reserve mechanisms that only fail late. RR therefore rises early and is a core component of the UK NEWS2 track-and-trigger score, where it carries heavy weighting.

Rising RR often precedes a cardiac arrest by 6–8 hours, giving a window to intervene.
It requires no equipment — only a watch and observation.
Commonly under-recorded or guessed (“18” written by default), which loses this warning.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — counting correctly

Count breaths over a full 60 seconds — do not count for 15 seconds and multiply, as this magnifies error and misses irregular patterns (e.g. Cheyne-Stokes). Observe the rise and fall of the chest or abdomen with the patient at rest. Classically it is done discreetly, immediately after taking the pulse with your hand still on the wrist, so the patient is unaware and does not consciously alter their breathing.

Note depth, rhythm and effort, not just the number.
Assess in a position of comfort; agitation or talking falsely raises the count.
3INTERPRETATION — normal, tachypnoea & work of breathing

Normal adult RR is 12–20 breaths/min. Both extremes matter: tachypnoea signals distress or acidosis, while a falling rate can herald exhaustion or CNS/opioid depression. Look actively for signs of increased effort.

RR 12–20/min→Normal range
RR 21–24/min→Tachypnoea — NEWS2 score 2, review
RR ≥ 25/min→NEWS2 score 3 — significant distress, escalate
RR ≤ 8/min→NEWS2 score 3 — consider opioid/CO₂ narcosis, exhaustion
Accessory muscle use / tracheal tug→Severe increased work of breathing

Recognisable signs of increased work of breathing:

💪Accessory muscles
Sternocleidomastoid & scalenes active at rest
🔻Tracheal tug
Downward pull of trachea on inspiration
📉Recession
Intercostal / subcostal in-drawing (esp. children)
👃Nasal flaring
Widening nostrils to cut airway resistance
🪑Tripod position
Leaning forward on arms to fix shoulder girdle
👄Pursed lips
Splints airways open in COPD (auto-PEEP)
4ABNORMAL PATTERNS & PITFALLS

The rhythm of breathing carries diagnostic information beyond rate alone.

Kussmaul (deep, sighing, fast)→Metabolic acidosis — classically DKA, uraemia
Cheyne-Stokes (crescendo-decrescendo with apnoea)→Heart failure, stroke, raised ICP, end of life
Agonal (slow, gasping, irregular)→Peri-arrest — start resuscitation, NOT normal breathing
Prolonged expiratory phase / wheeze→Obstructive airways disease (asthma, COPD)

Common causes of tachypnoea: pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, asthma/COPD, sepsis, metabolic acidosis (DKA, lactic), anxiety, pain, anaemia and fever. Pitfalls: a normal RR does not exclude hypoxia; SpO₂ can stay near-normal from compensatory tachypnoea until sudden collapse. Pulse oximetry is a poor substitute for counting effort and rate.

🚩 A rising RR is often the earliest sign of impending arrest. Beware the tiring patient whose rate is now falling toward normal with worsening distress or drowsiness — this is exhaustion, not improvement. A silent chest in acute asthma (no wheeze, minimal air entry) or agonal gasps are pre-arrest emergencies demanding immediate senior and critical-care help.
🎓 RR is the single earliest vital sign to change in deterioration — before pulse, BP or GCS. In OSCEs and on the ward, always count for a full minute and record the actual number; a genuine RR of 22 buried in the notes may be the only clue that a patient is heading for the ICU.

Pulse oximetry (SpO₂) is a non-invasive bedside measurement of arterial oxygen saturation. A probe passes red (660 nm) and infrared (940 nm) light through a pulsatile vascular bed (finger, ear, toe) and calculates the percentage of haemoglobin saturated with oxygen from the differential absorption of the pulsatile (arterial) component. It gives a continuous, real-time estimate of oxygenation, but it measures saturation only — not ventilation, not the partial pressure of oxygen, and not the type of haemoglobin present.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently: oxyHb absorbs more infrared and lets red through (so oxygenated blood looks red), while deoxyHb absorbs more red. The device samples absorption many times per second and isolates the pulsatile arterial signal from the constant tissue/venous background, calculating the ratio and converting it to a saturation reading.

Used universally: acute assessment, anaesthesia, ward observations (part of NEWS2), oxygen titration and monitoring of any breathless or unwell patient.
Relies on the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve — the sigmoid relationship between SpO₂ and arterial PaO₂.
The curve is flat at the top: above ~90% large falls in PaO₂ produce only small falls in SpO₂, so a "normal-ish" saturation can mask a substantial drop in PaO₂.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Place the probe on a warm, well-perfused digit or ear lobe. Ensure a good plethysmographic (pulse) waveform or a strong signal-quality indicator — a reading without a reliable trace is meaningless. Remove nail varnish or false nails and allow the reading to stabilise. Document the inspired oxygen (air or the flow/FiO₂) alongside the value, because a saturation is only interpretable if you know what the patient is breathing.

Correlate with the palpated pulse rate — if the displayed rate does not match the patient, distrust the number.
In poor peripheral perfusion an ear-lobe or forehead probe may perform better than a cold finger.
3INTERPRETATION & TARGETS

For most acutely unwell adults the target range is 94–98%. Patients at risk of hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure — classically COPD and other chronic CO₂ retainers — have a lower target of 88–92% to avoid abolishing hypoxic respiratory drive and worsening CO₂ retention.

≥96% on air→Normal oxygenation in a healthy adult
94–98%→Standard target range for most acutely ill patients
88–92%→Target in COPD / CO₂ retainers at risk of type 2 failure
<90% (approx PaO₂ 8 kPa)→Respiratory failure — steep part of the curve, deterioration accelerates
Falling trend despite oxygen→Escalate, check ABG, seek senior help
4PITFALLS & UNRELIABLE READINGS

Anything that degrades the pulsatile signal or alters light absorption can give a false or absent value.

🩸Poor perfusion
Shock, hypotension, cold peripheries or vasoconstriction lose the pulsatile signal — low or absent reading
💅Nail varnish
Dark/blue varnish and false nails absorb light and can falsely lower or obscure the value
🤸Motion
Shivering, tremor or movement artefact produces erratic, unreliable readings
🎨Skin pigmentation
Darker skin tones tend to OVER-estimate true saturation, risking occult (hidden) hypoxaemia
☠️Carboxyhaemoglobin
CO poisoning — COHb absorbs like oxyHb, so SpO₂ reads FALSELY NORMAL despite tissue hypoxia
🟤Methaemoglobin
Methaemoglobinaemia drives the reading toward a fixed ~85% regardless of true saturation
Normal SpO₂ but drowsy, cherry-red, headache→Suspect CO poisoning — needs co-oximetry / ABG
Reading "stuck" near 85%, cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood→Suspect methaemoglobinaemia
🚩 A normal SpO₂ does NOT exclude carbon monoxide poisoning — the oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and will read reassuringly high while tissues are hypoxic. If CO exposure is suspected (fire, faulty boiler, headache in multiple household members), give high-flow oxygen and measure COHb on a co-oximeter or arterial blood gas. Remember too that SpO₂ reflects oxygenation only, NOT ventilation: a patient can maintain a normal saturation on oxygen while dangerously retaining CO₂ and becoming acidotic — only an ABG reveals this.
🎓 The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve underlies every reading: it is sigmoid and flat above 90%, so SpO₂ is an insensitive marker of early deterioration at the top end but falls steeply once it drops below ~90% (roughly PaO₂ 8 kPa). Rightward shift (fever, acidosis, high CO₂, raised 2,3-DPG) unloads oxygen to tissues; leftward shift (alkalosis, hypothermia, low CO₂, and crucially carboxyhaemoglobin) holds oxygen on and impairs delivery.

Body temperature measurement is a core vital sign that estimates thermal balance between heat production and loss. It screens for fever (a marker of infection/inflammation) and for hypothermia, guides sepsis recognition, and monitors response to treatment. The clinical value depends heavily on the SITE measured, because core temperature and peripheral (surface) temperature can differ substantially.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — core vs peripheral
Temperature is taken at every routine observation set (NEWS2), on admission, and whenever infection, hypothermia or a transfusion/drug reaction is suspected. The aim is to estimate CORE temperature — the tightly regulated temperature of vital organs and blood — set by the hypothalamus. Peripheral sites (skin, axilla) reflect surface temperature and underestimate core, especially when the patient is vasoconstricted or cold-exposed.
👂Tympanic
Infrared, ear drum shares blood supply with hypothalamus — fast, good core proxy if technique correct
👅Oral
Sublingual pocket; close to core but affected by drinks, breathing and probe placement
💪Axillary
Peripheral; convenient/safe but reads ~0.5–1°C BELOW core — least accurate
🌡️Rectal
Closest to true core; reference in severe hypothermia & children, but invasive and lags on rapid change
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — technique & preparation
Tympanic: gently pull the pinna up and back to straighten the canal, aim the probe at the drum, use a clean cover. Wax, poor angle or a short insertion falsely LOWERS the reading.
Oral: place probe in the posterior sublingual pocket with lips closed; wait if the patient has recently eaten, drunk or smoked.
Axillary: probe in the centre of a dry axilla with the arm held firmly against the chest wall for the full dwell time.
Rectal: reserved for neonates/young children and suspected severe hypothermia where surface sites are unreliable.

Document the SITE alongside the value, and trend using the SAME site where possible so changes are comparable.

3INTERPRETATION — normal ranges & thresholds
36.1–37.2°C→Normothermia (typical adult range; diurnal variation, lowest early morning, highest late afternoon)
≥38.0°C→Fever / pyrexia — regulated rise in hypothalamic set-point (infection, inflammation, malignancy, drugs)
>40.0°C→Hyperpyrexia — medical emergency; consider CNS infection, drug/serotonin toxicity, heat stroke, thyroid storm
<35.0°C→Hypothermia (core)
32–35°C→MILD hypothermia — shivering, tachycardia, confusion
28–32°C→MODERATE — shivering stops, bradycardia, reduced consciousness, arrhythmia risk
<28°C→SEVERE — coma, fixed dilated pupils, VF/asystole risk; may mimic death

In NEWS2, both high (≥38.1) and low (≤36.0, and especially ≤35.0) temperatures score points, reflecting that deviation in EITHER direction is significant.

4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SEPSIS SIGNIFICANCE
Recent HOT or COLD drinks, eating or smoking distort ORAL readings for several minutes — wait 15–30 min or use another site.
Poor TYMPANIC technique (wax, wrong angle, cerumen, otitis) and axillary UNDER-estimation are common sources of falsely low values.
A single reading is a snapshot — trend matters; environmental exposure, sweating and antipyretics all shift the value.
In SEPSIS the temperature may be HIGH, but in the elderly, neonates, or immunosuppressed it can be NORMAL or LOW; hypothermia in sepsis carries a worse prognosis.
🚩 Normothermia does NOT exclude sepsis. Elderly, neonatal, and immunosuppressed patients may be afebrile or hypothermic despite severe infection — a temperature of <36°C in an unwell patient is an ominous, not a reassuring, sign. Assess the whole picture (NEWS2, lactate, mentation), not the temperature alone.
🎓 Fever is a REGULATED rise in the hypothalamic set-point driven by pyrogens (e.g. IL-1, IL-6, TNF, prostaglandin E₂) and is lowered by antipyretics. HYPERTHERMIA (heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, serotonin/neuroleptic malignant syndrome) is UNregulated heat gain overwhelming dissipation — the set-point is normal, so antipyretics do NOT work and active cooling ± specific antidotes are needed.

Capillary refill time (CRT) is a rapid bedside test of peripheral perfusion: you blanch the skin or a nailbed with firm pressure, release, and time how long the colour takes to return. A normal central CRT is under 2 seconds; prolongation suggests impaired perfusion from shock, hypovolaemia or dehydration, and it is most valuable as part of the paediatric “end of the bed” assessment of a sick child.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Used in any acutely unwell patient as a quick screen of circulatory status — part of the “C” in an A–E assessment and of the paediatric assessment triangle.
Principle: applying pressure empties the superficial capillary bed; on release, the speed of reperfusion reflects local blood flow and cardiac output. Poor perfusion (vasoconstriction, hypovolaemia, shock) slows the return of colour.
Especially useful in children, in whom compensated shock maintains blood pressure until late — so perfusion signs like CRT change before hypotension appears.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Press firmly on a nailbed (peripheral) or, preferably, over the sternum (central) for 5 seconds.
Release the pressure and count the seconds until normal colour returns to the blanched area.
Central CRT (sternum, forehead) is more reliable than peripheral CRT because it is less affected by ambient temperature and peripheral vasoconstriction.
Elevate a peripheral site (e.g. finger) slightly above heart level when testing to standardise venous drainage.
🎓 A common exam trap: peripheral CRT at the fingertip is easily prolonged by a cold room alone — always specify and prefer the sternal (central) CRT in a shocked patient.
3INTERPRETATION
Central CRT < 2 seconds→Normal peripheral perfusion
CRT ≥ 2 seconds (prolonged)→Possible poor perfusion — hypovolaemia, dehydration or shock; assess in context
Prolonged CRT + tachycardia + cool mottled peripheries in a child→Compensated shock — escalate, give fluids, reassess
Prolonged CRT + reduced skin turgor + dry mucous membranes→Significant dehydration (paediatric assessment)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
🌡️Cold ambient temperature
Peripheral vasoconstriction falsely prolongs CRT
🦵Peripheral vascular disease
Local arterial disease slows refill independent of shock
📉Poor sensitivity in adults
Unreliable and observer-dependent — never diagnostic alone
💡Lighting & nail varnish
Poor light or coloured nails obscure colour return
🚩 A prolonged central CRT alongside tachycardia, mottling and altered consciousness points to shock and demands urgent action — but never rely on CRT alone. A normal CRT does not exclude serious illness, so interpret it together with heart rate, blood pressure, mental state and urine output.
BEDSIDE TESTS__Point-of-Care Tests:
The 12-lead ECG is a non-invasive recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 different electrical "views" — 6 limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) looking at the heart in the vertical/frontal plane and 6 chest leads (V1–V6) looking in the horizontal plane. It is the single most important bedside cardiac investigation, used to diagnose acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, chamber hypertrophy and electrolyte/drug effects. Standard calibration is a paper speed of 25 mm/s (so 1 small square = 0.04 s, 1 large square = 0.2 s) and 10 mm/mV (2 large squares = 1 mV) — always check the calibration mark before interpreting.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The ECG detects the summed vector of myocardial depolarisation and repolarisation via skin electrodes. Each lead is a directional "camera": a wave of depolarisation moving towards a lead produces a positive (upward) deflection, and away produces a negative one. Indicated for chest pain, palpitations, syncope, breathlessness, suspected electrolyte disturbance, drug overdose, and pre-operative assessment.

Limb leads (frontal plane): I, II, III form Einthoven's triangle; aVR, aVL, aVF are the augmented leads.
Chest leads (horizontal plane): V1–V6 wrap around the anterior and lateral heart.
The heart's electrical axis (normal −30° to +90°) is derived mainly from leads I and aVF.
2CORRECT LEAD PLACEMENT

Accurate electrode placement is essential — misplacement is the commonest cause of a "pseudo-abnormal" ECG and can mask or mimic infarction.

🧪V1
4th intercostal space, right sternal edge
🧪V2
4th intercostal space, left sternal edge
🧪V3
Midway between V2 and V4
🧪V4
5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
🧪V5
Anterior axillary line, same level as V4
🧪V6
Mid-axillary line, same level as V4–V5
Limb electrodes: Red–Right arm, Yellow–Left arm, Green–Left leg, Black–Right leg (earth) — "Ride Your Green Bike".
Posterior leads V7–V9 and right-sided V4R are added when posterior or right ventricular infarction is suspected.
3SYSTEMATIC INTERPRETATION

Read every ECG the same way: rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR interval, QRS, ST segments, T waves, QTc.

Rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves→Normal 60–100 bpm; <60 bradycardia, >100 tachycardia
PR interval > 0.2 s (1 large square)→First-degree AV block
QRS ≥ 0.12 s (3 small squares)→Broad complex — bundle branch block or ventricular origin
Positive QRS in I, negative in aVF→Left axis deviation
Negative QRS in I, positive in aVF→Right axis deviation
QTc > 440 ms (men) / > 460 ms (women)→Prolonged QT — torsades risk
4KEY EMERGENCIES & TERRITORIES

STEMI is diagnosed by ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 2 contiguous limb leads, or ≥ 2 mm in ≥ 2 contiguous chest leads. The affected leads localise the culprit coronary artery.

ST elevation V1–V4 (anterior/septal)→Left anterior descending (LAD) artery
ST elevation II, III, aVF (inferior)→Right coronary artery (RCA)
ST elevation I, aVL, V5–V6 (lateral)→Left circumflex (LCx) artery
Tall R + ST depression V1–V3 (mirror)→Posterior MI — usually RCA/LCx
P waves and QRS completely dissociated→Complete (third-degree) heart block
Broad, regular, monomorphic tachycardia→Ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise
🚩 ST elevation on the ECG mandates immediate action: activate the primary PCI pathway without delay — "time is muscle". Equally, confirm correct lead placement before calling an ECG abnormal: a right-sided inferior STEMI (RCA) can cause hypotension with nitrates, and swapped limb electrodes (e.g. red/yellow) can mimic infarction or dextrocardia.
🎓 In inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF), always record a right-sided ECG (V4R): ST elevation in V4R indicates right ventricular infarction, meaning the patient is preload-dependent — give fluids and avoid GTN/nitrates and other preload-reducing drugs.

Capillary blood glucose ("BM") and capillary blood ketone testing are the workhorse bedside investigations of acute diabetes care. A finger-prick sample is applied to a reagent strip in a point-of-care meter, giving a glucose value in seconds and (on ketone-capable meters) a β-hydroxybutyrate level. Together they detect hypoglycaemia, quantify hyperglycaemia, and — with a venous gas — clinch the diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used for any acutely unwell patient, all diabetics, altered consciousness, sepsis, seizures, and drug/alcohol intoxication — hypoglycaemia is a rapidly reversible cause of coma that must never be missed. The strip contains glucose oxidase (or dehydrogenase); glucose in the sample drives an enzymatic reaction generating a small electrical current proportional to glucose concentration.

Capillary ketone strips measure β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB), the dominant ketoacid in DKA — more reliable than urine dipstick, which detects acetoacetate.
Point-of-care results guide immediate action but are screening tools, not the definitive laboratory assay.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Wash and dry the hands — remove any sugar/food residue that falsely raises the reading.
Use a fresh lancet on the side of a fingertip (less painful, better perfused); avoid the pulp centre.
Discard the first drop, apply the second hanging drop to the strip; do not squeeze/milk the finger (dilutes with tissue fluid).
Insert into a meter with an in-date, correctly-coded strip; a second strip on the same meter gives the ketone value.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
Fasting 4–7 mmol/L→Normal capillary glucose
<4 mmol/L→Hypoglycaemia — "4 is the floor", treat immediately
>11 mmol/L→Hyperglycaemia; check ketones if unwell/type 1
Ketones <0.6 mmol/L→Normal β-hydroxybutyrate
Ketones 0.6–2.9 mmol/L→Raised — emerging ketosis, recheck & act
Ketones ≥3 mmol/L→Significant ketonaemia — suggests DKA

The DKA diagnostic triad requires all three:

🩸Hyperglycaemia
Glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes)
🧪Ketonaemia
β-OHB ≥3 mmol/L or ketonuria ≥2+
🌡️Acidosis
pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Sugar/fruit contamination on an unwashed finger falsely elevates glucose — the classic spurious "high BM".
Poor peripheral perfusion (shock, hypothermia, vasoconstriction) makes capillary readings unreliable and often falsely low.
Extremes of haematocrit distort results — anaemia tends to over-read, polycythaemia to under-read glucose.
Meters are inaccurate at very high/very low glucose and are not validated for diagnosing diabetes — confirm on a venous laboratory sample.
🚩 A capillary glucose <4 mmol/L demands immediate treatment (oral fast-acting carbohydrate if conscious; IM glucagon or IV glucose if not) — do not wait for lab confirmation. Conversely, if the bedside value is discordant with the clinical picture, send an urgent paired venous lab glucose before acting on the number alone.
🎓 In DKA it is the ketonaemia and acidosis that define severity, not the glucose. "Euglycaemic DKA" — seen with SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy and starvation — shows raised ketones and acidosis with glucose that may be <11 mmol/L, so always check ketones in the unwell diabetic even when the BM looks reassuring.

A venous blood gas (VBG) is a rapid, point-of-care blood sample (usually peripheral venous, sometimes capillary) that gives an almost instant read-out of acid–base status and key metabolic markers — pH, pCO₂, bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), base excess, lactate, glucose, electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺) and haemoglobin. It is used to answer the bedside question “is this patient acidotic, and how sick are they metabolically?” within a minute — but it deliberately trades away reliable assessment of oxygenation.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

A VBG is drawn when you need fast metabolic information without arterial puncture. Venous blood, having passed through the tissues, carries slightly more CO₂ and is marginally more acidic than arterial blood, but for pH, bicarbonate and lactate the venous and arterial values track each other closely enough to guide management.

Sepsis / shock: a single venous lactate rapidly flags tissue hypoperfusion.
DKA: serial VBGs track pH, bicarbonate, ketones and potassium during insulin therapy.
Any unwell patient: quick screen for metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia or anaemia.

It avoids the pain, arterial spasm and bleeding risk of an arterial stab and can be taken from the same cannula as routine bloods.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Blood is collected into a heparinised syringe from a peripheral vein (often at cannulation) or as a capillary (arterialised) sample from a warmed heel/finger in neonates. The sample must be free of air bubbles, gently mixed to prevent clotting, and analysed promptly (ideally within minutes).

Avoid a prolonged tourniquet or repeated fist-clenching — stasis falsely raises K⁺ and lactate.
Delay or an air bubble alters pCO₂ and pO₂ and lets cells keep metabolising, raising lactate/K⁺.
The analyser measures pH and pCO₂ directly and calculates bicarbonate and base excess.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS

Interpret pH first, then the respiratory (pCO₂) and metabolic (HCO₃⁻/base excess) components, remembering the venous offsets.

Venous pH vs arterial→~0.03–0.04 lower than arterial (venous normal ~7.32–7.42)
Venous pCO₂ vs arterial→~1 kPa higher than arterial — do not read as true arterial CO₂
pH < 7.35 with low HCO₃⁻ (<22 mmol/L)→Metabolic acidosis (e.g. DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure)
pH < 7.35 with high pCO₂→Respiratory acidosis — but confirm CO₂ retention on ABG
Lactate > 2 mmol/L→Hypoperfusion / raised; ≥4 mmol/L signals severe sepsis / shock
Base excess < −2 mmol/L→Metabolic acidosis; base excess > +2 suggests metabolic alkalosis
🧪pH
Overall acid–base balance; reliable on a VBG
💨pCO₂
Respiratory component; venous runs ~1 kPa high
⚗️HCO₃⁻
Metabolic buffer; low in metabolic acidosis
🔥Lactate
Marker of hypoperfusion / anaerobic metabolism
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
No reliable oxygenation: venous pO₂ reflects tissue extraction, not lung function — never assess hypoxia from a VBG.
pCO₂ only a screen: a normal venous pCO₂ helps exclude hypercapnia, but a high value needs an ABG to confirm.
Sampling artefact: stasis, haemolysis or delay spuriously raise K⁺ and lactate.
🚩 A VBG cannot assess oxygenation — pO₂ and calculated saturation are unreliable. If hypoxia or significant CO₂ retention (type 1 or type 2 respiratory failure) is suspected, an arterial blood gas is mandatory. Use pulse oximetry alongside, and do not be reassured by VBG oxygen numbers.
🎓 A raised lactate (>2 mmol/L, and especially ≥4 mmol/L) is a key marker of tissue hypoperfusion and is embedded in the Sepsis Six — it stratifies severity and its clearance with resuscitation is a marker of response.

Body mass index (BMI) is a simple, cheap bedside anthropometric measure that relates a person's weight to their height to screen for underweight, healthy weight, overweight and obesity. It is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, and it underpins nutritional screening, obesity classification and estimation of surgical, anaesthetic and metabolic risk.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

BMI is used to screen whole populations and individuals for abnormal body composition and to track change over time. The underlying principle is that, across most adults, body weight scales approximately with the square of height, so dividing weight by height² gives a value that is largely independent of stature and can be compared against fixed WHO thresholds.

Formula: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Units are kg/m².
Worked example: a 70 kg adult who is 1.75 m tall has BMI = 70 ÷ (1.75 × 1.75) = 70 ÷ 3.06 ≈ 22.9 kg/m² (healthy weight).
Used in obesity clinics, pre-operative assessment, nutritional screening (as part of the MUST tool) and chronic-disease risk stratification.
2HOW IT IS MEASURED

Accuracy depends on standardised technique rather than self-report. Measure weight on calibrated scales with the patient in light clothing and no shoes, and height with a wall-mounted stadiometer, heels together, standing straight and looking at the horizon (Frankfort plane).

Waist circumference is measured at the midpoint between the lowest rib and the iliac crest, at the end of gentle expiration, as a complementary marker of central (visceral) adiposity.
Where height cannot be measured (bed-bound, contractures, kyphosis), use a surrogate such as ulna length or knee height, or recall of recent weight loss for the MUST score.
3INTERPRETATION — WHO CATEGORIES

The calculated value is mapped to fixed WHO categories. Obesity is further split into classes I to III, which guide the intensity of intervention including consideration of bariatric surgery.

BMI < 18.5→Underweight — assess for malnutrition / underlying illness
18.5–24.9→Healthy (normal) weight
25.0–29.9→Overweight — lifestyle advice, screen for comorbidity
30.0–34.9→Obesity class I
35.0–39.9→Obesity class II
≥ 40.0→Obesity class III (severe / morbid) — consider bariatric referral
≥ 23 (South Asian / Chinese)→Overweight equivalent — lower thresholds due to higher visceral fat & diabetes risk
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & CLINICAL USE

BMI is a screening tool, not a measure of body fat, and must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture and waist circumference.

💪Muscular athletes
High lean mass raises BMI without excess fat — falsely labelled obese
👵Elderly
Sarcopenia means normal BMI can hide low muscle & poor reserve
💧Oedema / ascites
Fluid overload inflates weight — BMI overestimates true mass
🤰Pregnancy
BMI invalid in pregnancy — use booking (pre-pregnancy) weight
📏Waist circumference
Adds central-fat risk (≥94 cm men, ≥80 cm women = raised risk)
🔪Surgical risk
High BMI raises anaesthetic, VTE, wound & airway risk peri-operatively
🚩 BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle or fluid, so a "normal" value never excludes malnutrition or disease. Treat unintentional weight loss of >5% in 3–6 months (or a MUST score ≥2) as a red flag for occult cancer or serious illness that mandates investigation, regardless of the absolute BMI. In the very frail, refeeding after prolonged starvation can precipitate refeeding syndrome — reintroduce nutrition slowly with electrolyte monitoring.
🎓 Remember the two "≥" numbers examiners love: obesity begins at BMI ≥30 (class III / severe at ≥40), and the overweight threshold drops to ≥23 in South Asian and Chinese populations because of higher visceral fat and type 2 diabetes risk at any given BMI.

Nasogastric (NG) tube placement confirmation is a bedside safety check performed before every use of a fine-bore feeding tube to prove the tip lies in the stomach and not the respiratory tract. The first-line test is aspiration of fluid onto a pH indicator strip: a pH of ≤5.5 confirms gastric placement and allows feeding, while any higher value or a dry tube mandates a second-line chest X-ray before anything is instilled. Misplaced NG feeding is a recognised NHS “Never Event.”

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Fine-bore NG tubes are inserted blindly and can pass into the trachea, bronchus or pleura without provoking obvious coughing, particularly in sedated, neurologically impaired or elderly patients. Instilling feed, water or drugs into a lung-sited tube causes catastrophic aspiration pneumonitis and death. Confirmation exploits the fact that resting gastric contents are strongly acidic (parietal-cell hydrochloric acid) whereas bronchial and pleural fluid are near-neutral to alkaline.

Check position after initial insertion, before each feed, before giving medication, and after vomiting, retching, coughing or suctioning.
Also re-check if the external tube length has changed or the tube appears displaced.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Using a syringe, gently aspirate 0.5–1 mL of fluid from the tube. Place a drop onto CE-marked pH indicator paper intended for human gastric aspirate (never blue litmus, which only distinguishes acid from alkali). Compare the colour against the reference chart and read the pH to within half a unit.

If no aspirate is obtained: turn the patient onto their side, advance or withdraw the tube 10–20 cm, inject 10–20 mL air, and wait 15–30 minutes before retrying.
In patients who are nil by mouth or on continuous feed, briefly pausing the feed helps acid re-accumulate.
3INTERPRETATION

The NPSA safe cut-off is a pH of 5.5 or below.

pH ≤5.5 on aspirate→Gastric placement confirmed — tube is SAFE to use
pH 6.0 (borderline/high)→Do NOT feed — wait, reposition and re-test; if still >5.5 request chest X-ray
No aspirate obtainable→Do NOT feed — reposition/wait; escalate to chest X-ray if still dry
Any doubt / high risk→Chest X-ray is the definitive second-line confirmation
🧪pH indicator strip
First-line test; CE-marked paper reading to 0.5 units
🩻Chest X-ray
Definitive second-line check; tip must sit below diaphragm
⛔Auscultation
The “whoosh” air test is unreliable and must NEVER be used
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Acid-suppressing drugs (proton-pump inhibitors, H₂ antagonists) and recent feed raise gastric pH above 5.5, causing false-negative results and unobtainable confirmation.
Respiratory or pleural aspirate can occasionally read in the 6–7 range but is never ≤5.5, which is why the low cut-off is protective.
A correct pH confirms gastric, not necessarily optimal, tip position; the X-ray also verifies depth and that the tube is not coiled.
🚩 NEVER feed, flush or give medication down an NG tube with a pH >5.5, no aspirate, or any uncertainty about position. NEVER rely on the auscultation “whoosh” test or bubbling in water — these are discredited. Feeding into a misplaced tube is a Never Event and can be rapidly fatal.
🎓 Memorise the number: pH ≤5.5 = safe to feed. It is the single most examined NG fact. If pH is above 5.5 or the tube is dry, the correct answer is always “do not feed — reposition/wait or obtain a chest X-ray,” never “auscultate.”

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and AVPU are bedside tools for objectively quantifying a patient's level of consciousness. GCS scores three responses — Eye opening (/4), Verbal (/5) and Motor (/6) — summing to a total of 3–15, where 15 is fully alert and 3 is deep coma. AVPU is a rapid four-point screen used in the primary survey. Both track trends in head injury, reduced consciousness and the acutely unwell patient, guiding airway decisions and escalation.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
GCS gives a reproducible, communicable measure of consciousness so that deterioration is detected early and objectively across different assessors. It is used in head injury, reduced/fluctuating consciousness, poisoning, stroke, sepsis and post-ictal states, and forms part of the ‘D’ (Disability) step of the ABCDE primary survey. The principle is that conscious level reflects the integrity of the brainstem reticular activating system and cortex; a falling score signals expanding pathology (haematoma, oedema, rising intracranial pressure) demanding urgent action. AVPU is the fast triage equivalent for the initial sweep.
2HOW IT IS SCORED
Assess the best response in each domain. Apply a standardised stimulus: voice first, then a peripheral then central painful stimulus (e.g. trapezius squeeze, supraorbital pressure) if needed.
👁️Eyes /4
4 spontaneous, 3 to voice, 2 to pain, 1 none
💬Verbal /5
5 orientated, 4 confused, 3 words, 2 sounds, 1 none
💪Motor /6
6 obeys, 5 localises, 4 withdraws, 3 flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
Total = E + V + M, range 3 (lowest) to 15 (normal).
Abnormal flexion (decorticate, score 3) vs abnormal extension (decerebrate, score 2) — extension is the more ominous.
Modify for confounders: intubated verbal is recorded as “T”; note if eyes swollen shut.
3INTERPRETATION & ACTION
Severity of head injury is conventionally banded by total GCS, but the trend and the component breakdown matter more than any single number.
GCS 13–15→Mild head injury / near-normal consciousness
GCS 9–12→Moderate — close monitoring, senior review, consider CT head
GCS ≤8→Severe / coma — airway at risk, call anaesthetics to secure it
Drop ≥2 points→Significant deterioration — urgent reassessment & imaging
AVPU ‘P’ or ‘U’→Roughly GCS ≤8 — treat as airway emergency
AVPU mapping: Alert ≈ 15, Voice ≈ 12–13, Pain ≈ 8, Unresponsive ≈ 3.
AVPU is for rapid triage; convert to a full GCS once time allows.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Confounded by intoxication, sedation, post-ictal state, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and dysphasia — correct reversible causes (check glucose) before attributing a low score to structural injury.
Inter-observer variability, especially for the verbal score in young children (use paediatric GCS) and intubated patients.
A single total hides the picture: E3 V4 M8 is impossible — always report each component so errors and localising signs are visible.
🚩 GCS ≤8 means the patient may be unable to protect their airway — secure it (definitive airway/intubation) and get anaesthetic help immediately. A falling GCS is a neurological emergency: it may signal an expanding intracranial haematoma or rising ICP and warrants urgent CT and neurosurgical discussion, not watchful waiting.
🎓 The best motor response is the single most prognostic component. Never document a bare total — always report the breakdown as E–V–M (e.g. “GCS 10: E2 V3 M5”) so trends and localising responses are transparent.
BEDSIDE TESTS__Cardiovascular Bedside:
The Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is a quick, non-invasive bedside test comparing systolic blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, using a hand-held Doppler probe. It is the first-line screening and severity tool for peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and, crucially, is mandatory before applying compression bandaging to a leg ulcer. The Toe-Brachial Index (TBI) is its companion when calcified, incompressible calf vessels make the ABPI unreliable.

1Indication & principle

In a healthy limb, ankle systolic pressure equals or slightly exceeds brachial pressure, so the ratio is around 1.0. A flow-limiting arterial stenosis drops the distal pressure, lowering the index. ABPI is used to screen for and grade PAD, investigate claudication or rest pain, and to confirm arterial adequacy before compression therapy.

ABPI = highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest brachial systolic pressure (calculated separately for each leg).
The ankle value uses the higher of the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial signals for that leg.
The brachial value is the higher of the two arms.
2How it is performed

The patient rests supine for 10-20 minutes (exertion or a recent cigarette falsely lowers readings). A sphygmomanometer cuff and a hand-held Doppler are used to record return-of-flow systolic pressures.

🩺Brachial
Doppler over brachial artery; inflate cuff, record pressure at which flow returns. Repeat both arms.
🦶Ankle
Cuff above malleoli; Doppler over dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial in turn. Take the higher.
🧮Calculate
Divide highest ankle by highest brachial for each leg to give a per-limb index.
3Interpretation
0.9-1.3→Normal arterial supply
0.5-0.9→Mild-to-moderate PAD; typically intermittent claudication
<0.5→Severe PAD / critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulcers, gangrene) — urgent vascular referral
>1.3→Falsely elevated — incompressible, calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD); result unreliable
4Pitfalls, TBI & safety

Medial arterial calcification stiffens the calf vessels so they resist cuff compression, giving a spuriously high or normal ABPI even in significant disease. When ABPI is unreliable (>1.3 or borderline in a diabetic/renal patient), measure the Toe-Brachial Index: the small digital arteries are relatively spared from calcification.

TBI < 0.7→Abnormal — indicates PAD when ABPI is falsely reassuring
Other pitfalls: inadequate rest, wrong cuff size, and severe ulceration/pain limiting cuff placement.
ABPI grades severity but does not localise the lesion — imaging (duplex/CTA) is needed for that.
🚩 Do NOT apply high-compression bandaging to a leg ulcer if ABPI <0.8 — compression on an ischaemic limb can precipitate tissue necrosis. A value >1.3 is falsely high (calcified vessels in diabetes/CKD) and does not exclude PAD — do not treat it as reassuring; use TBI instead.
🎓 A leg ulcer with ABPI 0.8-1.3 is safe for compression (venous picture); <0.8 flags an arterial or mixed component. Remember the diabetic trap: a "normal or high" ABPI with absent pulses and claudication should prompt a TBI, not false reassurance.

The hand-held Doppler is a continuous-wave (CW) ultrasound probe placed over a peripheral artery to listen to the pattern of blood flow. The shape and sound of the returning waveform reveal the health of the vessel and any upstream (proximal) disease: a crisp multiphasic signal reflects a healthy, elastic, unobstructed artery, whereas a dampened single-phase signal points to significant peripheral arterial disease (PAD). It is a cheap, non-invasive bedside tool used to assess arterial flow, calculate the ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI), locate vessels for cannulation, and help exclude venous thrombosis.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The probe emits a continuous ultrasound beam; moving red cells reflect it with a frequency shift (the Doppler effect) that is converted into an audible signal and a waveform. In a healthy limb, elastic arteries and high downstream resistance produce a characteristic multiphasic pattern. Disease upstream flattens this pattern.

Assessing arterial flow in suspected PAD or acute limb ischaemia.
Measuring ankle and brachial systolic pressures to derive the ABPI.
Locating an artery before arterial cannulation or checking a distal pulse that is impalpable.
Augmentation/compression assessment of veins when screening for DVT.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Expose the limb and warm the patient if possible (cold causes vasoconstriction and dampens signals). Apply acoustic gel and hold the probe at roughly 45–60° to the skin, angled towards the direction of flow, over the target vessel (e.g. dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, radial). Adjust position and angle until the clearest signal is heard.

Listen to the audible signal AND observe the waveform trace where available.
For ABPI: inflate a cuff proximally until the signal disappears, then deflate slowly and record the pressure at which flow returns.
Compare both limbs and multiple levels to localise disease.
3INTERPRETATION

The waveform is classified by the number of phases (components) per cardiac cycle. Loss of phases tracks worsening arterial disease.

Triphasic (forward systolic → brief reverse → forward diastolic)→Healthy, elastic, unobstructed vessel — normal
Biphasic (forward systolic + reverse, loss of the late forward component)→Loss of vessel compliance / early disease (can be a normal variant in older patients)
Monophasic (single forward flow, no reverse component, dampened)→Significant proximal stenosis / established PAD
Absent signal→Occlusion or critical/acute ischaemia — urgent vascular review
🔊Triphasic
Sharp "whoosh-whoosh" — normal artery
🔉Biphasic
Reverse flow lost — early stiffening
🥁Monophasic
Dull, dampened tone — significant PAD
🧮ABPI
0.9–1.3 normal; <0.9 PAD; ≤0.4 critical
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A signal being present does NOT mean flow is adequate — even a critically ischaemic limb may give an audible monophasic tone.
Calcified, incompressible vessels (diabetes, chronic kidney disease) give falsely high ABPI (>1.3); use toe pressures instead.
CW Doppler has no depth resolution and cannot distinguish overlapping vessels; it is operator-dependent.
Cold limbs, poor probe angle, and low cardiac output can all dampen the trace and mimic disease.
🚩 A monophasic signal indicates significant arterial disease with a proximal stenosis or occlusion — it must never be dismissed as reassuring simply because flow is audible. Combine with ABPI and clinical findings, and refer urgently if acute ischaemia is suspected.
🎓 Remember the progression: triphasic → biphasic → monophasic tracks worsening PAD. Each phase lost signals more severe or more proximal disease, so the number of waveform components is a quick bedside gauge of arterial health.

Four-limb blood pressure measurement records BP in both arms and both legs to detect a differential between upper and lower limbs (or between the two arms). It is a simple bedside test used chiefly to detect aortic coarctation, and also aids the assessment of aortic dissection and Takayasu arteritis. The key principle is that a fixed obstruction to flow along the aorta lowers the pressure distal to it, reversing or exaggerating the normal arm–leg relationship.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Performed when coarctation, dissection or a large-vessel arteritis is suspected: a young hypertensive, an unexplained murmur, absent/weak femoral pulses, radio-femoral delay, or acute severe chest/back pain. Normally the leg (ankle) systolic BP is equal to or slightly higher than the arm (ankle-brachial index ≥ 0.9–1.0) because of pulse-wave amplification in the periphery.

In coarctation a narrowing distal to the left subclavian obstructs flow to the lower body → high pressure above, low pressure below.
In dissection or Takayasu, asymmetric occlusion of a subclavian/brachiocephalic vessel produces an inter-arm difference.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

With the patient resting supine, measure systolic BP in sequence using an appropriately sized cuff for each limb:

Both arms (brachial artery) – compare left vs right.
Both legs (a large thigh cuff with popliteal auscultation, or ankle cuff with Doppler over posterior tibial/dorsalis pedis).

Use a cuff whose bladder encircles ~80% of the limb; a too-small thigh cuff falsely raises the leg reading. Simultaneously palpate the radial and femoral pulses together to detect radio-femoral delay.

3INTERPRETATION
Arm SBP > leg SBP with radio-femoral delay→Aortic coarctation
Arm–leg gradient > 20 mmHg (arm higher)→Significant coarctation
Inter-arm difference > 20 mmHg→Aortic dissection or subclavian stenosis
Reduced/unequal BP with bruits, young woman→Takayasu arteritis (“pulseless disease”)
Leg SBP ≥ arm SBP, no delay→Normal physiological pattern
🫀Coarctation
Arm > leg BP, radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension
🩸Dissection
Inter-arm difference > 20 mmHg, acute tearing pain
🧬Takayasu
Unequal/absent pulses, bruits, raised ESR in young women
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Wrong cuff size is the commonest error – a small thigh cuff over-reads and can mask a true arm–leg gradient.
A well-collateralised coarctation may show only a modest gradient at rest; the differential can widen on exertion.
If the coarctation is proximal and involves the left subclavian, the left arm BP is also low – always check the right arm.
🚩 A significant inter-arm difference (> 20 mmHg) or arm–leg gradient in a patient with acute severe chest/back pain must be treated as possible aortic dissection until excluded – arrange urgent CT aortogram and avoid delay.
🎓 The classic exam triad for coarctation is radio-femoral delay + arm BP higher than leg BP + upper-limb hypertension in a young patient. Remember the normal pattern is the opposite: leg ≥ arm.

The lying-and-standing blood pressure test (active stand test) is a simple bedside investigation to detect orthostatic (postural) hypotension — a sustained fall in blood pressure on standing that reflects failure of the normal baroreflex to defend perfusion against gravity. It is a core part of the assessment of dizziness, unexplained falls, and syncope, and it identifies a reversible, often drug-related cause of morbidity in older and diabetic patients.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

On standing, roughly 500–700 mL of blood pools in the legs and splanchnic bed. Normally the baroreflex triggers reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction to maintain cerebral perfusion. When this compensation fails, BP drops and the patient becomes symptomatic.

Investigate dizziness on standing, unexplained falls, syncope or pre-syncope.
Screen patients on antihypertensives, diuretics or vasodilators, and those with diabetes or Parkinson’s.
Assess suspected volume depletion or autonomic failure.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Standardised timing is essential — a hurried measurement misses delayed drops.

Rest the patient supine (lying) for ≥5 minutes, then record BP and heart rate.
Ask the patient to stand; measure BP at 1 minute and again at 3 minutes of standing.
Keep the cuff at heart level and record any symptoms (dizziness, visual greying, light-headedness) at each stage.
3INTERPRETATION

A positive test is a sustained postural fall within 3 minutes of standing, or reproduction of the patient’s symptoms.

Systolic drop ≥20 mmHg on standing→Orthostatic hypotension — positive
Diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg on standing→Orthostatic hypotension — positive
Fall <20 systolic / <10 diastolic, no symptoms→Negative — normal baroreflex response
Postural drop with rise in HR >30 bpm→Suggests hypovolaemia (intact reflex)
Drop with blunted / no HR rise→Suggests autonomic failure

The common causes cluster into a few groups:

💧Hypovolaemia
Dehydration, bleeding, diuresis — reflex tachycardia present
💊Drugs
Antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, TCAs
🧠Autonomic failure
Diabetic neuropathy, Parkinson’s, multiple system atrophy
🩺Adrenal insufficiency
Addison’s — consider with hyponatraemia, pigmentation, fatigue
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
Measuring too early misses delayed orthostatic hypotension — always take the 3-minute reading.
A single normal test does not exclude the diagnosis; symptoms often vary with time of day, meals and hydration.
Frail patients may be unable to stand safely — have a chair ready and stop if pre-syncope occurs.
🚩 A symptomatic postural drop is a major falls and syncope risk. Review culprit medications (diuretics, antihypertensives, nitrates), correct volume depletion, and put falls-prevention measures in place rather than dismissing the dizziness.
🎓 Remember the threshold precisely: a fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic OR ≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension — a favourite exam number.

Ambulatory and home blood pressure monitoring measure BP outside the clinic to confirm true hypertension, stripping out the artificial "white-coat" rise many patients show in a consulting room. NICE mandates that a raised clinic reading (≥140/90 mmHg) be confirmed by ABPM (24-hour automated) or, if that is declined/not tolerated, HBPM (self-measured at home) before hypertension is diagnosed and lifelong treatment started. The ambulatory/home average also uncovers masked, nocturnal and non-dipping patterns that a single clinic reading misses.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

A clinic BP is a single snapshot taken in an anxiety-provoking setting. Out-of-office monitoring gives many readings across the patient's normal day, so the average reflects true habitual BP and correlates better with cardiovascular outcomes than clinic readings.

Confirm a new diagnosis when clinic BP is ≥140/90 mmHg (and below 180/120).
Exclude white-coat effect (raised in clinic, normal outside) so patients are not treated unnecessarily.
Detect masked hypertension (normal in clinic, raised outside), nocturnal hypertension and non-dipping.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
🩺ABPM
Cuff worn 24h; automated readings ≥2 per hour during waking hours. Use the average of ≥14 daytime readings.
🏠HBPM
Two consecutive seated readings 1 min apart, twice daily (morning & evening), for ≥4 (ideally 7) days.
🧮AVERAGING
HBPM: discard day 1, average all remaining readings. ABPM: use the daytime (waking) mean for diagnosis.

The patient keeps a normal routine but must hold the arm still and at heart level when the cuff inflates. HBPM requires a validated, correctly-sized upper-arm device.

3INTERPRETATION — NICE THRESHOLDS

The out-of-office threshold is lower than the clinic threshold by roughly 5 mmHg, because the white-coat effect is removed.

Clinic ≥140/90 with ABPM/HBPM daytime avg ≥135/85→Stage 1 hypertension
Clinic ≥160/100 with ABPM/HBPM daytime avg ≥150/95→Stage 2 hypertension
Clinic ≥180/120→Severe hypertension — do NOT wait for ABPM; assess for same-day specialist/urgent review
ABPM/HBPM daytime avg <135/85 despite raised clinic BP→White-coat hypertension — not diagnosed, monitor
Night-time BP falls <10% below daytime mean→Non-dipper — higher cardiovascular risk
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Atrial fibrillation and frequent ectopics make oscillometric readings unreliable — use manual auscultation.
A cuff that is too small over-reads; ensure correct bladder size.
ABPM can disturb sleep, altering the nocturnal profile; some patients cannot tolerate it, hence HBPM as the alternative.
HBPM depends on patient technique and honest reporting; averaging ≥4 days reduces error.
🚩 White-coat hypertension means a normal ambulatory average must NOT be dismissed as trivial — these patients still need periodic review as many progress to sustained hypertension. Conversely, masked hypertension (normal clinic BP, raised ABPM/HBPM) is dangerous precisely because clinic readings falsely reassure while end-organ damage accrues — consider it in patients with hypertensive target-organ damage but normal clinic BP.
🎓 Learn one number: 135/85 mmHg is the daytime ABPM/HBPM threshold for stage 1 hypertension (matching clinic 140/90), and 150/95 matches clinic 160/100 for stage 2. If asked why the ambulatory figure is lower, the answer is removal of the white-coat effect.

Vagal manoeuvres are bedside techniques that transiently boost parasympathetic (vagal) tone to slow atrioventricular (AV) nodal conduction. They are the first-line, non-pharmacological intervention for haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). They serve a dual role: they may terminate AV-node-dependent re-entrant tachycardias (AVNRT and AVRT), and where they fail to terminate they may transiently slow the ventricular rate to unmask the underlying atrial rhythm (e.g. flutter waves).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Used for the acute management of stable, regular, narrow-complex SVT before adenosine.
Mechanism: raising intrathoracic/carotid baroreceptor pressure → reflex ↑ vagal (parasympathetic) output → slowed conduction through the AV node.
Because AVNRT and AVRT use the AV node as an obligatory limb of the re-entry circuit, transient AV block can break the circuit and restore sinus rhythm.
AVNRT / AVRT (AV-node dependent)→may TERMINATE — abrupt return to sinus rhythm
Atrial flutter / atrial tachycardia→transient ↑ AV block UNMASKS flutter (sawtooth) waves — diagnostic, not curative
Sinus tachycardia→gradual transient slowing then speeds back up — no termination
2MODIFIED VALSALVA (REVERT technique)
Sit the patient semi-recumbent (~45°). Ask them to blow into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger — generating ~40 mmHg pressure — for 15 seconds.
Immediately lay the patient flat and a colleague performs a passive leg raise to 45° for 15 seconds. This augments venous return and the baroreceptor-mediated vagal surge.
Return the patient to semi-recumbent and reassess the rhythm after ~45 seconds.
Modified (postural) Valsalva→~43% cardioversion to sinus rhythm (REVERT trial)
Standard supine Valsalva→only ~17% success — the modified technique is markedly superior
3CAROTID SINUS MASSAGE (CSM)
Auscultate for a carotid bruit first — if present, do NOT proceed.
Patient supine with neck slightly extended and rotated away. Locate the carotid sinus at the level of the upper thyroid cartilage, just below the angle of the jaw.
Apply firm circular pressure over ONE side only for 5–10 seconds under continuous ECG monitoring. Never massage both sides simultaneously.
If unsuccessful, the contralateral side may be tried after a short interval — but only one side at any one time.
Ventricular pause ≥ 3 seconds or drop in systolic BP ≥ 50 mmHg→carotid sinus hypersensitivity (relevant in syncope work-up)
4SAFETY, PITFALLS & CONTRAINDICATIONS
🩸Carotid bruit
Absolute contraindication to CSM — embolic stroke risk
🧠Recent TIA / stroke
Avoid CSM within the preceding 3 months
💓Instability
Shock, ischaemia, HF or ↓BP → go to synchronised DC cardioversion, not manoeuvres
⚠️Digoxin toxicity
Relative contraindication — risk of provoking dangerous bradyarrhythmia
Always perform with continuous ECG monitoring, IV access, and resuscitation facilities available.
Record a 12-lead ECG (or a rhythm strip during the manoeuvre) — capturing the moment of AV block or termination is diagnostically valuable.
🚩 NEVER perform carotid sinus massage if there is a carotid bruit or a history of TIA/stroke in the last 3 months — dislodging an atheromatous plaque can cause an embolic stroke. Massage one side only, never both together, and only under continuous ECG monitoring with resuscitation equipment to hand.
🎓 For a stable, regular narrow-complex SVT the exam-correct FIRST step is the modified Valsalva manoeuvre (strain semi-recumbent, then flat with passive leg raise) — ~43% success vs ~17% for the standard technique — before moving on to IV adenosine.
