The digital rectal examination (DRE) is a fundamental bedside test in which a gloved, lubricated index finger is inserted into the rectum to assess the anal canal, rectum, prostate (in men) and pelvic floor. It is quick, cheap and requires no equipment, yet it yields critical diagnostic information across urology, colorectal surgery, gastroenterology and neurology – from characterising the prostate and detecting melaena to assessing anal tone in suspected cauda equina syndrome.

1INDICATIONS & PRINCIPLE

The examining finger reaches roughly 7–10 cm into the rectum, allowing direct palpation of the prostate anteriorly, the rectal mucosa circumferentially, and the anal sphincter. Inspection of glove contents (blood, stool colour) adds further information. It is indicated across several distinct clinical scenarios.

🧪Prostate
LUTS, retention, suspected prostate cancer – assess size, surface, consistency
🩸GI bleed
PR bleeding or suspected melaena – inspect stool on glove
🚽Bowel habit
Change in bowel habit, low rectal mass, faecal impaction
🧠Neuro
Suspected cauda equina / cord compression – anal tone & perianal sensation
Also used for acute urinary retention (impaction as a cause), anal/perianal pathology (fissure, abscess, fistula, haemorrhoids), and to obtain stool for testing.
In suspected cauda equina, DRE assessing anal tone and perianal (S2–S4) sensation is a mandatory part of the examination, never to be skipped.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, and always offer a chaperone (documenting their name). Position the patient in the left lateral position with hips and knees flexed toward the chest.

Inspect first: part the buttocks and inspect the perianal skin for skin tags, external haemorrhoids, fissures, fistula openings, excoriation, prolapse or masses.
Palpate: place a gloved, well-lubricated index finger on the anal verge, and with gentle pressure insert through the sphincter. Assess resting tone, then sweep circumferentially through the rectum.
Prostate (men): palpate anteriorly for the two lateral lobes and the central median sulcus, noting size, surface, consistency and tenderness.
Withdraw & inspect: examine the glove for blood, mucus and stool colour (fresh blood vs black tarry melaena).
🎓 Ask the patient to squeeze your finger to assess voluntary sphincter contraction (a marker of external sphincter / pudendal integrity), distinct from resting tone.
3INTERPRETATION OF FINDINGS

The classic clinical value of DRE lies in distinguishing benign from sinister prostate findings, and in the tone/sensation examination that flags a surgical emergency.

Smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery prostate; sulcus preserved→Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Hard, craggy, irregular / nodular prostate; loss of median sulcus→Prostate cancer until proven otherwise – urgent suspected-cancer referral
Exquisitely tender, boggy, warm prostate→Acute prostatitis (avoid vigorous massage – bacteraemia risk)
Black, tarry, offensive stool on glove→Melaena – upper GI bleed (proximal to caecum)
Reduced / absent resting anal tone + saddle anaesthesia→Cauda equina syndrome – emergency MRI
Hard palpable stool filling the rectum→Faecal impaction (a treatable cause of overflow incontinence & retention)
Empty, ballooned rectum with obstruction→Suggestive of proximal obstructing lesion
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
DRE assesses only the distal ~10 cm; a normal DRE does not exclude higher rectal or colonic pathology – it complements, never replaces, endoscopy.
A normal-feeling prostate does not exclude cancer (many tumours are impalpable), and DRE cannot reliably size the prostate – correlate with PSA and imaging.
DRE can transiently raise serum PSA; where both are needed, take PSA before or defer sampling for about a week after examination.
Relative cautions: recent anorectal surgery, severe neutropenia, and vigorous prostate massage in acute prostatitis.
🚩 In suspected cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression, DRE to assess anal tone and perianal (S2–S4) sensation is mandatory and time-critical – never omit it. Reduced tone or saddle anaesthesia mandates emergency MRI and urgent surgical referral to prevent irreversible bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction. Equally, never omit DRE in a suspected GI bleed – melaena on the glove may be the first objective evidence.

Fundoscopy (direct ophthalmoscopy) is a bedside examination of the retina, optic disc and retinal vessels using a handheld ophthalmoscope. It is a core neurological and general-medicine skill, most importantly used to detect papilloedema — bilateral optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure (ICP) — as well as hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy and emboli.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The optic nerve head is the only part of the central nervous system visible directly through the transparent ocular media. Because the subarachnoid space is continuous around the optic nerve, a rise in intracranial pressure is transmitted to the nerve, obstructing axoplasmic flow and venous return → the disc swells. Fundoscopy therefore gives a non-invasive window onto ICP and onto systemic vascular disease.

Suspected raised ICP: headache, vomiting, visual obscurations, focal deficit, before lumbar puncture.
Systemic screening: hypertension, diabetes, endocarditis (Roth spots), stroke/TIA (emboli).
Acute visual loss or unexplained neurological presentation.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Darken the room to encourage natural pupil dilatation; if permitted and there is no suspicion of acute raised ICP needing serial pupil checks, dilate with tropicamide 1% for the best view. Ask the patient to fixate on a distant point and ignore the light.

Use your right eye/hand for the patient's right eye, and left for left, to avoid bumping noses.
Set the dial to +10 and start ~30 cm away to check the red reflex, then move in following a vessel back to the disc.
Systematically assess: optic disc (margins, colour, cup), vessels (calibre, AV crossings, pulsation), macula (ask patient to look at the light), then the four peripheral quadrants.
3INTERPRETATION — DISC & RETINAL FINDINGS

Papilloedema is bilateral disc swelling due to raised ICP; the classic signs progress over time.

Blurred nasal then whole disc margins + hyperaemic disc→Early papilloedema
Loss of spontaneous venous pulsation at disc→Early sign of raised ICP (absent in ~20% normally)
Paton lines (concentric retinal folds around disc)→Established papilloedema
Elevated disc obscuring vessels + peripapillary haemorrhages→Fully developed / chronic papilloedema
AV nipping, silver wiring, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots→Hypertensive retinopathy
Microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, neovascularisation→Diabetic retinopathy
White-centred retinal haemorrhages (Roth spots)→Infective endocarditis, leukaemia, anaemia
4DIFFERENTIALS & PITFALLS OF DISC SWELLING

Not every swollen-looking disc is papilloedema; distinguish true swelling from mimics and from unilateral optic nerve pathology.

🧠Papilloedema
Bilateral, raised ICP, vision usually preserved early (enlarged blind spot)
⚡Papillitis
Optic neuritis; usually unilateral, painful eye movements, marked visual loss + RAPD
🩸Ant. ischaemic optic neuropathy
Pale swollen disc, sudden altitudinal loss; think GCA
🟡Pseudopapilloedema
Optic disc drusen / hypermetropia mimicking swelling; no obscuration of vessels
🔴Central retinal vein occlusion
Unilateral disc swelling with widespread "stormy sunset" haemorrhages

Pitfalls: undilated pupils, media opacity (cataract), patient movement, and mistaking a myopic tilted disc or drusen for true swelling. A small cup, absent venous pulsation and vessel obscuration favour true papilloedema.

🚩 Papilloedema means raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise. Arrange urgent neuroimaging (CT/MRI head) to exclude a mass or hydrocephalus. Do NOT perform a lumbar puncture before imaging when papilloedema is present — removing CSF with an obstructing lesion risks fatal brain herniation (coning).
🎓 Loss of spontaneous venous pulsation is one of the earliest signs of raised ICP — but remember it is normally absent in up to 20% of healthy people, so its absence alone is not diagnostic, whereas the reappearance of pulsation reliably indicates normal pressure.

The Sit-Up-Squat-Stand (SUSS) test is a rapid bedside assessment of proximal muscle strength used to gauge medical risk in patients with severe eating disorders. Profound undernutrition causes a proximal myopathy: the large muscles of the hips, thighs and trunk waste and weaken. The SUSS test unmasks this weakness by asking the patient to rise from lying and from squatting without using their arms, scoring each manoeuvre 0–3. A low score is an objective marker of dangerous physical compromise and forms a core component of the MEED / MARSIPAN medical risk framework alongside BMI, heart rate, blood pressure and biochemistry.

1Indication & principle

Severe malnutrition depletes muscle mass and impairs the metabolic function of remaining fibres, producing a proximal myopathy that preferentially affects antigravity muscles (hip and knee extensors, trunk flexors). Because these are the muscles used to sit up and to stand from a squat, testing them at the bedside gives a quick, reproducible surrogate for whole-body physical deterioration.

Used in anorexia nervosa and other restrictive eating disorders to stratify medical risk (MEED guidance, formerly MARSIPAN).
Cheap, quick and repeatable — ideal for serial monitoring of the same patient over hours to days.
Complements — never replaces — BMI, bradycardia, postural blood pressure and electrolytes.
2How it is performed

Two manoeuvres are tested. Explain and demonstrate first, and ensure a safe environment (firm surface, someone nearby to guard against a fall).

🛏️Sit-up
Patient lies flat and sits up to a seated position without using hands or arms.
🧎Squat-stand
Patient squats down then rises to standing without using hands or arms or pushing on the thighs.

Each manoeuvre is scored independently on a 0–3 scale:

Score 3→No difficulty at all
Score 2→Able, but noticeably difficult (visible effort / slow)
Score 1→Able only by using hands / arms for leverage
Score 0→Unable to complete the manoeuvre at all
3Interpretation & risk

The lower the score, the weaker the proximal musculature and the higher the medical risk. Any need to use the arms, and certainly any inability to rise, signals a patient who is physically compromised.

Score 3 (each task)→Normal proximal strength — low concern on this parameter
Score 2→Alert / moderate concern — monitor closely and repeat
Score ≤ 1→High medical risk — significant proximal myopathy
Score 0 (unable to rise unaided)→Very high risk — escalate for urgent medical review / admission
4Pitfalls & limitations
Not specific to malnutrition — coexisting arthritis, injury, obesity or a primary neuromuscular disorder can independently lower the score.
Effort-dependent: a distressed or ambivalent patient may under-perform, so interpret alongside objective observations.
A single normal SUSS score does not exclude high risk — a patient can be dangerously bradycardic or hypokalaemic yet still rise unaided.
Best used as a trend: a falling serial score is a strong signal of deterioration.
🚩 Inability to sit up or stand without using the arms (score 0–1) reflects severe proximal myopathy and marks a physically high-risk patient who needs urgent medical assessment and usually admission. Do not reassure on BMI alone. These patients are also at major risk of refeeding syndrome — feeding must be cautious with electrolyte (phosphate, potassium, magnesium) monitoring and replacement, as an unmonitored refeed can precipitate fatal hypophosphataemia and cardiac failure.
🎓 In the MEED / MARSIPAN framework the SUSS test turns an abstract idea — "how weak is this patient?" — into a bedside number. A classic exam vignette is the low-BMI patient who can only stand by pushing on their thighs (score 1): quote the SUSS score as objective evidence of high medical risk rather than relying on BMI alone.
